newsitem.title: UK: Britain bids brutal farewell to outgoing PM Major.
newsitem.headline: Britain bids brutal farewell to outgoing PM Major.

text.p: As a triumphant Tony Blair swept into Downing Street on Friday, Britain's outgoing prime minister John Major slipped quietly away, stripped of official home, car and privilege just one day after crushing defeat at the polls.
In the time it takes to stage a military coup, the handover of power in Britain was complete.
Major was yesterday's man.

"Just as he loses his car, he will have to pay for the move. It is a rough world now for him," said Michael Gerson, head of the removal company that hauled out the Majors' belongings as the victorious Blairs strode in the front door.
Major and his wife Norma had just 24 hours to vacate the official residence at 10 Downing Street, a house they had called home for more than six years.
Few nations are so brutal in casting out their figureheads.
A defeated U.S. president has 11 weeks to wind up affairs at the White House and adjust to civilian life.
Outgoing presidents in South Korea get more than two months' grace and Italy can take months to install a new prime minister.
From New Zealand to Canada, ex-leaders are given about a week to clear out belongings, and perhaps only in coup-ridden Africa are handovers so brutal as in democratic Britain.

"You're beat and you're out. It's rather like a heavyweight contest -- once you get knocked out you just get carried from the ring as quickly and decently as possibly," said Joe Haines, who was press secretary to former prime minister Harold Wilson.

In just one day in 1970, Wilson went from being the most important man in Britain to a homeless has-been. He refused to go house-hunting before the election for fear pundits would label him a loser before the polls had even opened.
The only softening of the blow was one final stay at the prime minister's official country residence, Chequers, before those keys too were reclaimed for the incoming tenant.
Wilson's successor Edward Heath fared no better at the next election, when he too found himself with nowhere to live. It fell to an adviser, Sir Timothy Kitson, to lend his boss a home.
"It's a terrible system. The prime minister must be the one person in this country who can be thrown out of his house in about 24 hours," Kitson told BBC television.
In just one day, life turned upside down.
"I remember -- from a Jaguar (car) we moved down to a rather dilapidated Morris Oxford, Kitson said."
Clementine Churchill, wife of the war-time leader, positively feared humdrum reality after her privileged life.
"We shan't even have a car. We are being lent one now. We are learning how rough and stony the world is," she said.
Lord Healey well remembers the poignancy of his boss James Callaghan being ousted by Margaret Thatcher in 1979 -- and the sun vanishing for what seemed like an age.

"You're supposed to leave the moment the election result is known," Healey said. "I was able to take a photo of Jim leaving No. 10 in a glorious burst of sunlight and Maggie arriving within the hour -- in a deep gloom."
Yet even "Iron Lady" Thatcher had to face the ignominy of being turfed out of the house she believed was hers by right upon relinquishing power in 1990.
In her memoirs, Thatcher recalls nipping downstairs from the Downing Street flat to check she had left nothing in her study before leaving for the very last time.
"It was a shock to find I could not get in because the key had already been taken off my key ring," Thatcher wrote.
Her removal man Graham Green recalls a frenetic job.

"It was very hectic, very hectic," he told BBC television. "One minute she's there and the next minute she's gone. And we've got two days to get it all out. All them years of gifts and what not -- there was a lot of ornaments."
